arguments.title: Deterministic mutation-killing suite for task-runner.mjs
arguments.spec:
# Spec: Deterministic mutation-killing test suite for src/task-runner.mjs

Deliverable: test/agent/**/*.test.js (plus shared, non-test helper seam modules under test/agent/) and tests/manifest.json (schemaVersion 1, complete becomes true only in the last card). src/task-runner.mjs is correct and FROZEN -- write tests, never change it.

Nine mutants in mutants/m1..m9 each change exactly one behaviour of runWithRetry, mapWithConcurrency or createCancellation. npm test runs the agent's suite twice per claimed mutant (once against real src/, once against the mutant) and once against real src/ alone as a baseline; a claimed mutant that survives, or a baseline failure, fails the build.

The module never reads a clock or creates a timer -- sleep is injected, the cancellation token is built by the caller, and the worker is the caller's own function -- so the suite must be fully deterministic: no setTimeout/setInterval/setImmediate/Date.now()/performance.now(), no reading mutants/, no Function.toString(). Ordering and concurrency are driven through two shared seams built in the first two implementation cards: a recording sleep fake (records requested delays, resolves immediately) and a deferred+tracked-worker pair (a manually-resolved promise per call, plus an in-flight counter) that makes overlap and out-of-order settlement observable without any race.
arguments.plan:
1. retry-attempt-count-and-backoff-schedule: build the sleep-recording seam, kill m1/m2/m3.
2. cancellation-timing-and-late-subscriber: kill m4/m9, reusing the sleep seam for the mid-backoff cancel.
3. concurrency-result-ordering: build the deferred/tracked-worker seam, kill m5.
4. concurrency-peak-limit: reuse the deferred/tracked-worker seam, kill m6/m7/m8.
5. mutation-suite-completeness-pass: confirm all nine, set complete: true.
All five touch the shared tests/manifest.json (and cards 2-4 each reuse a seam module the prior card built), so they are chained strictly sequentially -- never parallel.
arguments.summary: Writes a deterministic test suite that kills all nine planted mutants of the retry/cancellation/concurrency module, in five sequential cards: build the timing seam and cover attempt count + backoff (m1-m3), cover cancellation timing and late-subscriber notification (m4, m9), build the concurrency seam and cover result ordering (m5), cover peak concurrency (m6-m8), then a final completeness pass.

tasks.title: Build the sleep-recording seam; test attempt count and backoff schedule (kills m1, m2, m3)
tasks.prompt:
runWithRetry(operation, { attempts, backoffMs, sleep, cancellation }) in src/task-runner.mjs calls operation(attempt) up to `attempts` times, awaiting sleep(backoffMs * 2 ** (attempt - 1)) between tries (no backoff after the last attempt).

Step 1 -- build the shared seam every later card in this plan reuses. Create test/agent/seams.js (plain ESM, no test framework import needed in this file) exporting createRecordingSleep(): returns { sleep, calls } where `sleep` is `async (ms) => { calls.push(ms); }` -- it records the exact delay requested and resolves immediately, so the suite never waits on real time and stays fully deterministic.

Step 2 -- write test/agent/retry-timing.test.js (plain ESM, node:test + node:assert/strict) with at least two tests:
1. Attempt count (kills m1): with attempts: 3 and an operation that fails on every call, assert the operation was called EXACTLY 3 times and the promise rejects with the operation's own last error. The mutant runs the loop with `attempt < attempts` instead of `attempt <= attempts`, so it calls the operation only 2 times -- your assertion on the exact call count must catch that.
2. Backoff schedule (kills m2 and m3 with one assertion): with backoffMs: 10 and attempts: 4 and an operation that always fails, use createRecordingSleep() as the injected `sleep` and assert `calls` deep-equals EXACTLY [10, 20, 40] -- three entries, doubling from the first backoff, and nothing after the last attempt. m2 shifts the exponent (2 ** attempt instead of 2 ** (attempt - 1)), producing [20, 40, 80]; m3 removes the 'no backoff after the last attempt' guard, producing a 4th trailing entry. An exact deep-equal on the full array, not just its length or first value, is what separates the correct schedule from both mutants.

Update tests/manifest.json: add killed entries for m1, m2, m3, each with a `why` (>=12 chars) naming the specific behavioural difference (loop bound / exponent / trailing backoff). Leave `complete: false` -- this is not the last card. Run npm test and confirm your suite passes against the real src/ and the verifier reports m1, m2, m3 as killed.

tasks.title: Test cancellation-mid-backoff and late-subscriber notification (kills m4, m9)
tasks.prompt:
Two independent behaviours of the cancellation token in src/task-runner.mjs:

1. Cancellation timing in runWithRetry (kills m4): cancellation is checked before every attempt (`if (cancelled) throw new CancelledError();`), so a token cancelled while a backoff is in flight must stop the NEXT try and reject with CancelledError specifically -- not the operation's own error. Write this deterministically: reuse createRecordingSleep() from test/agent/seams.js (extend it if useful, e.g. an optional onCall hook invoked with the requested delay before the recorded sleep resolves), call runWithRetry with attempts: 3 and an operation that fails on its first call, and from inside the sleep seam's hook (i.e. exactly when the backoff after attempt 1 is requested) call `cancellation.cancel()` before letting the fake sleep resolve. Assert the overall call rejects with an error whose `name` is 'CancelledError' (or `instanceof` the exported CancelledError), and that the operation was called EXACTLY once -- never a second time. The mutant removes the pre-attempt cancellation check entirely, so it would call the operation again and either succeed or reject with a different error.

2. Late-subscriber notification on createCancellation() (kills m9): registering a listener via onCancel AFTER the token is already cancelled must fire that listener immediately -- a late subscriber must not miss an event that already happened. Write a direct unit test: create a token, call cancel() first, then call onCancel(listener) and assert the listener was invoked (synchronously, before the assertion runs). The mutant adds the late listener to the internal set instead of firing it, so it is silently never called -- your assertion must actually check the listener ran, not merely that no error was thrown.

Update tests/manifest.json: append killed entries for m4 and m9 (why >= 12 chars each) to the existing array from the previous card -- do not remove or alter its m1/m2/m3 entries. Run npm test and confirm all five mutants recorded so far (m1, m2, m3, m4, m9) are reported killed.

tasks.title: Build the deferred/tracked-worker seam; test result ordering under concurrency (kills m5)
tasks.prompt:
mapWithConcurrency(items, worker, limit) in src/task-runner.mjs must file each result under its INPUT index (`results[index] = value`) regardless of the order calls actually settle in.

Step 1 -- extend test/agent/seams.js with a deferred helper: createDeferred() returns { promise, resolve } where `resolve` is captured from `new Promise((r) => { resolve = r; })`. This lets a test hold a worker call open exactly as long as it chooses, with no real timer, and control the order in which concurrent calls settle -- the only way to make out-of-order settlement deterministic instead of a race.

Step 2 -- write test/agent/result-ordering.test.js: call mapWithConcurrency with at least 2 items and limit >= 2, where each item's worker awaits its own deferred. Start the call, let both workers begin (e.g. await a microtask tick such as `await Promise.resolve()` so both pump() loops have called worker() and are awaiting their deferred), then resolve them OUT OF ORDER -- the LATER item's deferred first, the EARLIER item's second. Await the overall mapWithConcurrency result and assert the returned array is still in exact input order (results[0] is item 0's value, results[1] is item 1's value), not settlement order. The mutant files each result under `results[next - 1]` instead of `results[index]`; because `next` keeps advancing as other pump() loops claim later items while this call's own worker is still awaiting its deferred, `next - 1` no longer matches this call's own index once completion order and input order diverge -- your out-of-order resolution is exactly what exposes that.

Update tests/manifest.json: append a killed entry for m5 (why >= 12 chars) to the existing array -- do not remove or alter the m1/m2/m3/m4/m9 entries. Run npm test and confirm all six mutants recorded so far are reported killed.

tasks.title: Test peak concurrency is exactly `limit` (kills m6, m7, m8)
tasks.prompt:
mapWithConcurrency(items, worker, limit) must never let more than `limit` calls to `worker` be in flight at once, including when there are fewer items than the limit allows.

Reuse createDeferred() from test/agent/seams.js (built by the previous card) plus a small in-flight counter: wrap the worker so it increments a counter on entry, awaits its own deferred, then decrements on exit, tracking the peak value the counter reaches.

Write test/agent/peak-concurrency.test.js with at least two tests:
1. With limit: 2 and 4 items (more items than the limit), let all eligible workers start (a microtask tick), then assert the peak in-flight count is EXACTLY 2 -- never more -- before resolving any deferred and letting the call complete. m6 starts limit + 1 runners (peak would reach 3); m7 starts one runner per item regardless of limit (peak would reach 4, i.e. items.length); m8 awaits each pump() in the runner-start loop instead of letting them run concurrently, collapsing execution to sequential (peak would never exceed 1). An exact equality on the peak count, not just an upper bound, is what separates the correct behaviour from all three.
2. With limit: 5 and only 2 items (fewer items than the limit allows), assert the peak in-flight count is EXACTLY 2, matching items.length rather than limit -- this is the 'including when there are fewer items than the limit allows' case the module's own docstring calls out, and a suite that only tests the items > limit case can miss a mutant that only misbehaves in this direction.

Update tests/manifest.json: append killed entries for m6, m7, m8 (why >= 12 chars each) to the existing array -- do not remove or alter the m1/m2/m3/m4/m5/m9 entries. Run npm test and confirm all nine mutants are now reported killed, but leave `complete: false` -- the completeness pass is the next card.
